chunks: "Copper wins for the conductors; gold wins as a thin protective finish. Electrically gold is actually worse: its resistivity is about 2.
4 times ten to the minus eight ohm-metres against 1. 7 for copper, so a gold trace of the same size has about 45% more resistance.
It's also vastly more expensive, thousands of times per unit mass and about twice as dense, so a board built with gold traces would cost hundreds of dollars in metal alone.
What gold does well is that it's noble: it doesn't oxidise or tarnish, so it stays solderable and keeps low, stable contact resistance.
That's why pads get a finish like ENIG, electroless nickel with an immersion gold layer only about 0. 05 to 0. 1 microns thick, and why edge connectors and contacts use gold.
The nickel underneath is a barrier that stops copper diffusing through the gold.
Gold has downsides too: it's soft, it dissolves into solder, and too much gold in a solder joint, a few percent by weight, makes it brittle.
And at GHz the nickel under the gold adds loss. So: copper for the current path, a thin gold finish where oxidation, flatness or contact life matter."
